messages.content: Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6.

function.name: statistics_calculate_p_value
function.description: Calculate the p-value for a t-test on a single sample from a population. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

sample_mean.description: The mean of the sample data. This is a float type value.

population_mean.description: The mean of the population data. This is a float type value.

sample_std_dev.description: The standard deviation of the sample data. This is a float type value.

sample_size.description: The size of the sample data.

two_tailed.description: Whether the test is two-tailed. If not provided, default is true.

message.content:
**Standard‑error (the “standard deviation” of the sampling distribution under H₀)**  

For a one–sample *t*‑test you compare the observed sample mean \(\bar{x}\) against the hypothesised population mean \(\mu_0\).  
Under \(H_{0}: \mu=\mu_0\), the sampling distribution of \(\bar{x}\) has a **mean** equal to \(\mu_0\) and a **standard deviation** (often called the *standard error*):

\[
SE_{\bar x}= \frac{s}{\sqrt{\,n\,}}
\]

where  
\(s\) – sample standard deviation (used as an estimator of the population SD when σ is unknown)  
\(n\) – sample size.

---

### Plugging in your numbers

| Symbol | Value |
|--------|-------|
| Sample mean (\(\bar{x}\)) | 98.2 |
| Population mean under \(H_0\) (\(\mu_0\)) | 98.6 |
| Sample standard deviation (\(s\)) | 1.4 |
| Sample size (\(n\)) | 40 |

Compute the denominator first:

\[
\sqrt{n} = \sqrt{40} \approx 6.32495
\]

Now divide the sample SD by this factor:

\[
SE_{\bar x}
   = \frac{1.4}{6.32495}
   \approx 0.2215
\]

So the **standard deviation of the null-hypothesis test’s sampling distribution**—i.e., the standard error—is approximately **0.22**.

> **Result:** \(SE_{\bar x} \;\approx\; 0.22\)

This figure is what you'd use in constructing the *t*-statistic:
\[
t = \frac{\bar{x}-\mu_0}{SE_{\bar x}} 
    = \frac{98.2-98.6}{0.2215}
    \approx -1.81 .
\]
If you need further help interpreting this *t*‑value or computing a p‑value, just let me know!
